facts.text: The squashed, stretched-looking opening titles are deliberate: a joke on old VHS copies of widescreen kung-fu movies, whose titles were squeezed to fit TV screens.
The film was first called "The Blade" until New Line Cinema sent a cease-and-desist. The Hollywood Stock Exchange then ran a title contest with about 4,000 entries and picked Six-String Samurai.
Director Lance Mungia started with Loyola Marymount film-school friends, each reportedly chipping in about $20,000. They headed to Death Valley to shoot what they thought would be a tiny action film.
Buddy's look began with director Lance Mungia's taped-up glasses. Star Jeffrey Falcon tried them on during a late-night writing break and looked like Buddy Holly, so a rock 'n' roll samurai was born.
The ruined 1890s bank on screen is in Rhyolite, Nevada, a real ghost town. The same ruins later turned up in Michael Bay's 2005 sci-fi film The Island.
Buddy brags about his "1957" hollow-body guitar, but the prop is really a mid-1960s Martin GT-series hollow-body. It's a small anachronism in a movie set in an alternate 1957 apocalypse.
Star Jeffrey Falcon reportedly wore Buddy's battered tuxedo for eight months of production without washing it, which helps explain the authentically wasteland look.
Jeffrey Falcon, who plays Buddy, did all his own stunts and sword fights with no wires or special effects. He was a martial artist, not a stuntman.
Director Lance Mungia's film-school short A Garden for Rio screened at Sundance. That got him the funding to finish Six-String Samurai.
Death, played by Stephane Gauger, is a parody of Guns N' Roses guitarist Slash. Gauger, born in Vietnam, later became a director and cinematographer. He died in January 2018.
Before this film, star Jeffrey Falcon was on the US Wushu team and made Hong Kong action movies in the 1980s and early 90s, like Licence to Steal and Outlaw Brothers.
Shooting in Death Valley at 116 degrees was brutal. The production reportedly lost four assistant cameramen to heat stroke.
The gravel-voiced DJ "The Werewolf" spoofs legendary 1950s radio DJ Wolfman Jack, who was also known for his growl.
Russian rockabilly-surf band Igor & The Red Elvises supply most of the soundtrack and appear on screen. One member plays an electric balalaika, a big triangular Russian instrument.
Jeffrey Falcon didn't just star as Buddy. He also co-wrote the film, choreographed the fights, and handled production design and costumes.
The cannibal suburban family sends up 1950s sitcoms like Leave It to Beaver, which is where the name Ward Cleaver comes from.
The crew shot on expired Fuji film stock and a heavily discounted Panavision camera package. It began with no script, just a premise.
Justin McGuire, who plays The Kid, was still in school during production. The film could only shoot on weekends.
Six-String Samurai premiered at the 1998 Slamdance festival and won Best Editing and Best Cinematography. Fangoria, Film Threat and Ain't It Cool News all raved about it.
The film cost about $2 million but earned only $124,494 in its limited theatrical run. It became a cult favorite on home video instead.
The video game Fallout: New Vegas has an achievement called "New Vegas Samurai", for melee damage. Its icon is based on this film's poster.
"Follow the yellow brick road!" Besides that line, Lost Vegas looks like the Emerald City from a distance, and Death wants Buddy's guitar pick the way the Wicked Witch wanted Dorothy's slippers.
The ukulele-wielding guitarist is a riff on Ritchie Valens. Valens died in the 1959 plane crash that also killed Buddy Holly, the man Buddy is modeled on.
Film Threat gave Six-String Samurai a perfect five stars. Today it has a mixed 57% on Rotten Tomatoes.
In September 1998, Rob Liefeld's Awesome Entertainment published a one-shot Six-String Samurai comic. It was a continuation of the story, not an adaptation.
Variety's Leonard Klady called it "a rock 'n' roll Mad Max served up Cantonese style." The Village Voice's Laurie Stone called it derivative and repetitious.
Director Lance Mungia has a cameo as one of Death's bow-wielding archers.
Lance Mungia didn't direct another feature for seven years. His next was The Crow: Wicked Prayer (2005), the fourth Crow film. He made music videos in between.
The film openly spoofs The Road Warrior and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, as well as The Wizard of Oz.
The Village Voice's review said the film was "playing like an endless commercial for bullet-hole chic." It still praised one sequence's "vaudeville grace."
A no-budget project became a $2 million movie when an upstart distributor bought it in a reported seven-figure deal after Slamdance.
Some of the Russian Army brawl was barely choreographed. Reportedly one stretch was shot in two takes of ad-libbed moves.
The Soviet soldier doing the "tiger claw" is played by Noel Falcon, star Jeffrey Falcon's real-life brother.
Six-String Samurai is name-checked in later movies, including Three Kings (1999) and Gladiator (2000), as well as the video game Fallout: New Vegas.
The film got its first HD release in 2021 from Vinegar Syndrome, with new commentaries from director Lance Mungia and cinematographer Kristian Bernier.
Look for duct tape visible through the rips in Buddy's jacket, holding the arrows to his back.
For this duel, the prop swords were reportedly left behind. The first half was filmed with real swords and a Chinese sword champion until the prop truck arrived.
Six-String Samurai was meant to be the first of a trilogy. The sequels never happened, and neither did the big career launch some predicted for star Jeffrey Falcon.
In the credits, Red Elvises member Zhenya Kolykhanov is misspelled "Zhenga." A voice then says, "That's a wrap, baby!"
